      Abstract
Tape diagrams provide a graphical representation for arrows of rig categories, namely categories
equipped with two monoidal structures, ⊕ and ⊗, where ⊗ distributes over ⊕. However, their
applicability is limited to categories where ⊕ is a biproduct, i.e., both a categorical product and
a coproduct. In this work, we extend tape diagrams to deal with Kleisli categories of symmetric
monoidal monads, presented by algebraic theories.

 1      Introduction

Motivated by the growing interest in formal languages that are both diagrammatic and
compositional, an increasing number of works [1, 7, 8, 16, 24, 25, 28, 48, 50, 6] leverage string
diagrams [40, 52]. These diagrams formally represent arrows in a strict symmetric monoidal
category freely generated by a monoidal signature. A symbol s in the signature is depicted
as a box     s   , and arbitrary string diagrams are constructed through horizontal (;) and
vertical (⊗) composition of such symbols.
    While string diagrammatic languages are typically expressive enough to represent all
relevant systems, they often become cumbersome when dealing with control. For example,
representing quantum control within the ZX-calculus [15, 17] or probabilistic control of
Boolean circuits [49] requires ingenuity. Various works [57, 59, 55, 58, 2] adopt a hybrid
approach combining diagrammatic and algebraic syntax. Others [22, 38, 54] extend beyond
monoidal categories to rig categories [45, 39], roughly categories equipped with two monoidal
products, ⊗ and ⊕, where ⊗ distributes over ⊕.

           A key challenge in visualizing arrows in rig categories arises from the need to compose them
       not only horizontally (;) and vertically (⊗) but also using the additional monoidal product
       ⊕. One natural approach, implemented by sheet diagrams [19], utilizes three dimensions. An
       alternative, which remains within two dimensions, is offered by tape diagrams [5].
           Intuitively, tape diagrams are string diagrams of string diagrams: the vertical compos-
       ition of inner diagrams represents ⊗, whereas the vertical composition of outer diagrams
       represents ⊕.

 7       Conclusions
In this work, we have extended the notion of tape diagrams in [5] to accommodate Kleisli cat-
egories of monoidal monads. To achieve this, we introduced fc-cd rig categories (Definition 12),
which govern the interactions between (natural) ⊕-monoids and ⊗-comonoids. We then
demonstrated that these Kleisli categories naturally form fc-cd rig categories (Proposition 15).
Furthermore, we observed that when a monoidal monad is equipped with an algebraic
presentation T = (Σ, E), the operations in Σ induce natural transformations within the
Kleisli categories (Proposition 20). These monoids, comonoids, and natural transformations
enabled us to define a 2-dimensional diagrammatic language for the morphisms of T-cd rig
categories freely generated by a monoidal signature Γ (Theorem 30). Collectively, our results
ensure that whenever Γ is interpreted within the Kleisli category of a monoidal monad, this
interpretation can be uniquely extended to a rig functor from the category of diagrams Tcd  Γ,T .
For example, by interpreting Boolean circuits in SetD≤ , we obtain a language that captures
the expressiveness of [49] while naturally incorporating probabilistic control (Example 31).
    This work opens several promising research directions. (a) Extending tape diagrams
with monoidal traces for ⊕ could enable the modeling of iteration and, potentially, the
development of program logics akin to [4], but tailored for effectful programs. The necessary
constraints on monads could be drawn from [36, 30]. (b) We aim to further explore the
connections with probabilistic Boolean circuits in [49]. Notably, an alternative encoding of
the calculus in [49] into PCA-tapes maps each wire to the identity tape of 2̃. We anticipate
that this may clarify links to the theory of effectus [13]. (c) Our current approach does not
accommodate the monad of convex sets of distributions, as it is not monoidal. To incorporate
probability and non-determinism, we may leverage the graded monad from [46] and extend
tape diagrams for graded monads similarly to the string diagrams in [51]. (d) As discussed
in Section 5.2, T-rig categories are enriched over models of T. Investigating whether our
tape diagrams provide a principled approach to enriching string diagrams – such as the one
proposed in [58] – represents another intriguing avenue for future research.
